one_liner: In-place parallel/sequential comparison sort beating std::sort via cache-efficient block-based samplesort partitioning.
what_it_does: Drop-in replacement for std::sort: ips4o::sort(begin, end[, comp]) sorts a random-access range sequentially, and ips4o::parallel::sort(begin, end[, comp][, thread_pool]) does the same across threads. Solves general-purpose in-place comparison sorting for arrays and vectors of any comparable type, including small fixed-size records and duplicate-heavy keys.
how_it_is_fast: Superscalar samplesort: recursively partitions the array in-place into many buckets per pass using a branchless decision tree over sampled splitters, then permutes elements block-by-block to stay cache-efficient without extra memory. It special-cases inputs with many equal elements to avoid pathological partitioning, and the parallel version dynamically load-balances buckets across threads.
when_to_use: Sorting large arrays/vectors of primitives, floats, or small records (Pair/Quartet/100-byte) in-place with no extra buffer
Multi-core machines where parallel::sort (OpenMP or std::thread + TBB) can use the extra cores for large inputs (roughly n >= 2^18)
Data with many duplicate keys or skewed distributions, which the branchless classifier handles without the usual pathological slowdown
Sequential drop-in replacement for std::sort on Linux/macOS with a C++14-capable GCC or Clang toolchain
when_not_to_use: Windows builds -- the README states the code does not currently compile on Windows
Very small inputs (n <= 2^15), where BlockQuicksort is faster per the record's caveats
Need a stable sort that preserves the relative order of equal keys -- not documented as stable, and in-place bucket permutation gives no such guarantee
Can't add TBB and libatomic (or -mcx16 / native 16-byte CAS) to the build -- parallel mode requires them; sequential-only mode is header-only with no dependencies
Sanitizer-clean concurrency required -- open, unresolved TSan-flagged data race in the parallel presort check (issue #3)

integration.dependencies: sequential: none. parallel: pthreads/std::thread, TBB, libatomic (or -mcx16 / native 16-byte compare-and-exchange)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (CMakeLists sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14); benchmarked with GCC 7.5.0, -march=native -O3
integration.platforms: Linux/macOS, GCC or Clang, x86-64 (16-byte CAS needed for fastest parallel mode); does not compile on Windows
integration.thread_safety: not documented beyond parallel::sort owning its own thread pool per call; issue #3 (open) reports a TSan-flagged data race in the parallel presort check (base_case.hpp isSorted, concurrent vector<bool> writes)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- sequential ips4o::sort(begin, end[, comp]) matches std::sort's signature exactly; parallel::sort is a separate call you opt into, not automatic

gotchas: Parallel mode needs 16-byte atomic compare-and-exchange (-march=native or -mcx16, plus -latomic) or it falls back to lock emulation and loses speed
CMake's IPS4O_OPTIMIZE_FOR_NATIVE defaults to ON (-march=native), which can produce binaries that crash on other CPUs if redistributed
Open, unresolved TSan-flagged data race in the parallel presort check (issue #3)
The ips4o/ips4o repo ships no benchmark code (only src/example.cpp); the paper's numbers come from the separate GPL-3.0 ips4o-benchmark-suite, which is not linked from the README
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick IPS4o over BlockQuicksort/quadsort/fluxsort when you need a parallel multi-core sort or must stay robust across many data types and skewed/duplicate-heavy distributions; pick those instead for a header-only, dependency-free sequential drop-in with a simpler build.
verified_claims_summary: On the four-machine benchmark suite (arXiv 2009.13569, GCC 7.5.0, -march=native -O3), sequential IPS4o averaged roughly 2x std::sort's throughput on double/uint64/uint32 keys (Table 1 'Total' slowdown factors 1.20-1.78 for IPS4o vs 2.47-3.93 for std::sort's libstdc++ introsort), and Fig. 11 shows std::sort off-plot and slower than IPS4o on uniform uint64 across all four machines (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, AMD EPYC Rome 7702P, 2x Xeon E5-2683 v4, 4x Xeon Gold 6138). The paper gives no direct parallel-vs-std::sort figure; its parallel speedups (8.37x-40.92x) are relative to sequential IPS4o, not std::sort.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-01-15) but the maintained successor to the deprecated SaschaWitt/ips4o fork; BSD-2-Clause and header-only for sequential use, so it is easy to vendor even without upstream activity.
